newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says Japan reform may slow growth - official.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Japan reform may slow growth - official.

text.p: President Bill Clinton told Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Japan's plans to reform its fiscal system could slow down economic growth and cause an increase in Tokyo's current account surplus, a Japanese spokesman told reporters Friday.
Clinton made the remarks at an official meeting with Hashimoto held earlier on Friday, said the spokesman, who briefed reporters on the meeting.
The spokesman also quoted Clinton as telling Hashimoto that Japan's fiscal reforms could stimulate protectionist moves in the United States.
Clinton said a return of Japan's trade surplus to the higher level seen in the past is undesirable, and could bring about difficult problems in bilateral trade negotiations.
Clinton earlier told a news conference that he and Hashimoto had agreed on the need for strong domestic demand-led growth in Japan and to avoid a significant increase in Japan's external surplus.
The spokesman said Hashimoto assured Clinton that Japan's trade surplus is unlikely to increase substantially over the long term, although it may show a rise temporarily.

The spokesman said Clinton called on trade negotiators of both countries to make further efforts to solve bilateral trade issues including telecommunications, market access, implementation of past trade agreements, and civil aviation.
The spokeman said the two leaders agreed to intensify talks on Japan's deregulation under a bilateral framework agreement.

The United States is expected to offer an official proposal for the new talks shortly, and the two countries are expected to draw up concrete plans on how to proceed with the talks by June, the spokesman said.
"The creation of a new forum to discuss Japan's deregulation is an effective way to help Tokyo draw up reform plans," a senior Japanese government official told Reuters.
The official added that Clinton and Hashimoto did not discuss the issue of foreign exchange rates at the formal meeting.
